reference.source: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
clinicalPearls: A benign but often misdiagnosed disorder linked to internal rectal (mucosal) prolapse and chronic straining, frequently with paradoxical pelvic floor contraction
Presents with rectal bleeding, mucus discharge, straining, a sense of incomplete evacuation, and sometimes the need to digitate to evacuate
Despite the name, lesions may be single or multiple and ulcerated, polypoid, or merely erythematous, typically on the anterior rectal wall a few centimetres above the anal verge
Biopsy shows the characteristic fibromuscular obliteration of the lamina propria, with smooth muscle extending upward between the crypts, and features of mucosal prolapse
Endoscopy with biopsy is essential to distinguish it from malignancy and inflammatory bowel disease, both of which it can mimic
First-line management targets the underlying evacuatory disorder: bulking agents, bowel retraining, and biofeedback to correct straining and dyssynergia
Surgery, such as rectopexy for overt or internal prolapse, is reserved for refractory cases or associated full-thickness prolapse
reference.pathophysiology: Solitary rectal ulcer syndrome arises from chronic mechanical trauma to the rectal mucosa, driven by internal intussusception or mucosal prolapse and repeated straining, often with paradoxical (dyssynergic) contraction of the puborectalis. The prolapsing mucosa is subjected to shear, ischaemia, and direct trauma, including self-digitation, producing ulceration, hyperaemia, or polypoid change. Histology reflects this, with fibromuscular obliteration of the lamina propria and derangement of the muscularis mucosae characteristic of mucosal prolapse. The name is a misnomer, as lesions vary in number and appearance.
additionalDifferentials: Inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis or Crohn's)
additionalInvestigations: Flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy with biopsy for diagnosis and to exclude malignancy
Histology demonstrating fibromuscular obliteration of the lamina propria
Defecography (fluoroscopic or MR) to demonstrate internal or external prolapse and evacuatory dysfunction
Anorectal manometry and balloon expulsion to assess dyssynergia
Endoanal ultrasound where sphincter or prolapse assessment is required
Colonoscopy to exclude synchronous colonic pathology
redFlags: An endoscopic appearance mimicking malignancy, making biopsy mandatory before treatment
Progressive bleeding, weight loss, or anaemia
Failure to heal despite treatment of the evacuatory disorder
Development of a stricture or mass
reference.prognosis: A benign condition, but frequently chronic and difficult to treat; symptoms improve with correction of straining and biofeedback in many patients, while refractory cases with prolapse may require surgery with variable success.
pitfalls: Mistaking the lesion for carcinoma or Crohn's disease, or the reverse, without biopsy
Treating the ulcer topically while ignoring the underlying evacuatory disorder
Overlooking dyssynergic defecation amenable to biofeedback
Proceeding to surgery without confirming prolapse on defecography
references: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
Keighley & Williams' Surgery of the Anus, Rectum and Colon
management: First-line conservative therapy targeting the evacuatory disorder: high-fibre diet, bulk-forming laxatives and adequate fluids to reduce straining
Behavioural bowel retraining with biofeedback to correct paradoxical (dyssynergic) pelvic floor contraction and discourage digitation
Patient education to stop straining and reduce time spent attempting to evacuate
Topical agents such as sucralfate, mesalazine or short-course corticosteroids to promote mucosal healing
Endoscopic surveillance with biopsy to confirm the diagnosis and exclude malignancy and inflammatory bowel disease
Surgical repair such as rectopexy for associated internal or overt prolapse, reserved for cases refractory to conservative measures
Refer to a colorectal and pelvic-floor multidisciplinary team for refractory or prolapse-related disease
